![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14230052/assets/d33f9b851125443ff738fa4c3aedcbeaf8a202d05caa06747e74262c0ae89bd9.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={e}^{2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{2\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2{e}^{2\theta }.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{2\theta })}^{2}+{(2{e}^{2\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{4\theta }+4{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{5{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}{e}^{2\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{\pi }-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{\pi }-1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })}^{2}+{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{2\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{\frac{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}{4(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{\frac{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(4-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{5-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={csc}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ for $\pi /3\le \theta \le \pi /2?$
questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={csc}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-3{csc}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({csc}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-3{csc}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{6}⁡\theta +9{csc}^{6}⁡\theta {cot}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{csc}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{cot}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{cot}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={\theta }^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{({\theta }^{2})}^{2}+{(2\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{4}+4{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}(4+{\theta }^{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\theta \sqrt{4+{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\theta \sqrt{4+{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\frac{{(4+{\theta }^{2})}^{3/2}}{3}|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{{({\pi }^{2}+4)}^{3/2}-8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
